title: Welcome to the chessboard
objectives: Identify the board's orientation and the two sides

steps.text: This is a chessboard. It has 64 squares, alternating light and dark. For now, the board is shown from White's side: White's pieces begin at the bottom.

Each player controls one side: White pieces and Black pieces. White always moves first. Notice how the two sides mirror each other — every piece on White's back row has a matching piece straight across on Black's back row.

steps.prompt: Tap the square where White's king begins.

hints.text: Look for White's king. It's the tallest piece with a small cross on top.
It sits on White's back row, right of center.
One more look at that square.

feedback.d1: That's the queen's starting square — she stands right next to the king.
feedback.default: That's not the king's starting square. Look for the tallest piece with a small cross.

steps.successExplanation: White's king begins on e1, between the queen and the bishop.

steps.prompt: Now find Black's king on your own, without hints.

feedback.d8: That's Black's queen — she stands right next to the king, same as on White's side.
feedback.default: Not quite. Remember how the two sides mirror each other: find White's king on e1, then look at the square directly across the board from it.

steps.successExplanation: Black's king begins on e8 — directly across the board from White's king on e1, since the two sides mirror each other.

steps.prompt: True or false: which side moves first can change from game to game.

feedback.default: Actually, it's always White who moves first — every single game, no exceptions. Players can agree on who plays White, but once that's settled, White always takes the opening move.

steps.successExplanation: Right — White always moves first. That never changes, no matter who's playing or which game it is.

steps.summary: You now know the board's orientation: White's pieces start at the bottom, and White always moves first. You found both kings — White's on e1, Black's on e8 — and saw how the two sides mirror each other. Next: naming every square by its file and rank, so you can talk about any move precisely.
